assignment.title: Radical Expressions
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.teacherNotes: Bluebonnet Algebra II — Radicals, Lesson 2 (Operations with Radical Expressions), TEKS A2.7G. “Simplify” answers are graded by value AND form: any arrangement of the simplified expression is accepted, but the expression retyped, a perfect power left under a radical, a radical left in a denominator, unlike-radical mistakes, or a calculator decimal are marked not yet. Multi-step items ask for the intermediate step (the perfect-power factor, the multiplier, each FOIL product). Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

hints: Write {{k2}} and h^{{e}} as squares.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √(h⁴) is…

solutionReview.headline: Take the square root of each factor.
reasoning: So √({{k2}}h^{{e}}) = {{k}}h^{{f}}. No absolute value is needed: an even power is never negative.
solutionReview.commonError: Halving {{k2}} instead of taking its square root: √{{k2}} = {{k}}.

hints: A cube root of a negative number is negative: ∛(−8) = −2.
Write {{k3}}, a³ and y^{{e}} as cubes.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is the sign of the cube root of a negative number?

solutionReview.headline: Take the cube root of each factor.
reasoning: So ∛(−{{k3}}a³y^{{e}}) = −{{k}}ay^{{n}}: a cube root keeps the sign.
solutionReview.commonError: Only an even root of a negative number is not real; a cube root of a negative number is negative.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{(m {{c|signed}})^2}$. The variable $m$ can be any real number.
hints: Try a value of m that makes m {{c|signed}} negative. Is the square root negative?
For any real number u, √(u²) = |u|.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √((−3)²) equals…

solutionReview.headline: √(u²) = |u| for every real number u.
reasoning: Here u = m {{c|signed}}, which is negative for some values of m.
A square root is never negative, so √((m {{c|signed}})²) = |m {{c|signed}}|.
solutionReview.commonError: Without the bars, m {{c|signed}} is negative whenever m {{c|signed}} < 0, but a square root never is.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{25a^4b^9}$ with the Product Property. First write the radicand as (largest perfect-square factor) × (what is left).

steps.title: Product Property of Radicals
steps.instruction: ⁿ√(ab) = ⁿ√a · ⁿ√b when the roots are real. Split the radicand into an nth-power factor and what is left.

steps.title: Simplest radical form
steps.instruction: The index is as small as possible; the radicand has no factor (other than 1) that is an nth power; the radicand has no fractions; no radical is left in a denominator.

steps.title: Even roots and absolute value
steps.instruction: An even root is never negative. When an even root leaves a variable with an odd exponent outside, write it with absolute value bars: √(x²) = |x|.

hints: Find the largest perfect square in each factor: the number, each even power, and the even part of b⁹.
Use √(xy) = √x · √y: the perfect-square part comes out of the radical, and the rest stays under it.

solutionReview.headline: Take the square root of the perfect-square factor.
reasoning: b is left under the radical.
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving b⁹ = b⁸ · b partly under the radical, as in 5a²b³√(b³): b² is still a perfect square.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The square root of b⁸ is…

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[3]{125m^{30}p^{20}}$. Write the radicand as (largest perfect-cube factor) × (what is left).
hints: For a cube root, look for exponents that are multiples of 3.
Split p²⁰ into the largest multiple-of-3 power times what is left.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Under a cube root, which exponents come out evenly?

solutionReview.headline: Take out the largest perfect cube.
reasoning: 125 = 5³, m³⁰ = (m¹⁰)³, and p²⁰ = p¹⁸ · p² with p¹⁸ = (p⁶)³.
So the largest perfect-cube factor is 125m³⁰p¹⁸, and ∛(125m³⁰p¹⁸ · p²) = 5m¹⁰p⁶∛(p²).
solutionReview.commonError: Halving the exponents: a cube root takes a third of each exponent.

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[4]{625b^{28}k^{23}}$. Use absolute value where it is needed.

responses.label: Why is b⁷ written as |b⁷|?
options: b may be negative, so b⁷ may be negative, but a fourth root is never negative
Every variable outside a radical needs absolute value bars
responses.answer: b may be negative, so b⁷ may be negative, but a fourth root is never negative

hints: Write the number and each variable power as a fourth power times what is left.
k³ under a fourth root forces k ≥ 0, so k⁵ needs no bars.

solutionReview.headline: Pull out fourth powers; mind the sign.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing b⁷ without bars: b may be negative, so b⁷ may be too, and a fourth root is never negative. (k⁵ needs none: k³ under the radical forces k ≥ 0.)

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Can the fourth root of a real number be negative?

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{y^8}{x^7}}$. The Quotient Property gives $\dfrac{\sqrt{y^8}}{\sqrt{x^7}} = \dfrac{y^4}{x^3\sqrt{x}}$ — then rationalize the denominator.

responses.label: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by

hints: A radical left in a denominator is not simplest form.
Multiply the top and the bottom by the radical left in the denominator: a square root times itself is its radicand.

solutionReview.headline: Rationalize the denominator.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only the denominator by √x: the numerator needs the same factor, so y⁴ becomes y⁴√x.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is an expression with a radical in its denominator in simplest form?

questions.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{2}{9x}}$. Multiply inside the radical so the denominator becomes a perfect cube.

responses.label: Multiply the numerator and denominator of 2/(9x) by

hints: 9x = 3²x. A perfect cube needs 3³x³.
Multiply the top and the bottom by what completes 3³x³, then take the cube root of the denominator.

solutionReview.headline: Make the denominator a perfect cube.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying by 9x/9x makes 81x², which is not a perfect cube.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Under a cube root, what must the denominator become?

hints: ∛u · ∛v = ∛(uv) when the index is the same.
Multiply the radicands, then look for a perfect cube.

misconceptions.message: That is ∛(1000a³) — keep the coefficient 5 in front.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. When can ∛u · ∛v be written as ∛(uv)?
options: When the two indices are the same
scaffold.correct: When the two indices are the same

solutionReview.headline: Multiply under one cube root.
solutionReview.commonError: Stopping at 5∛(1000a³): 1000a³ is a perfect cube.

questions.prompt: Simplify $3\sqrt{45} - 5\sqrt{80} + 4\sqrt{20}$. Simplify each term first; only like radicals can be combined.

steps.title: Like radicals
steps.instruction: Like radical expressions have the same index and the same radicand: 3√5 and −7√5 are like; 3√5 and 3√2 are not.

steps.title: Add and subtract
steps.instruction: Simplify every radical first, then combine like radicals by adding their coefficients: 9√5 − 20√5 + 8√5 = (9 − 20 + 8)√5.

hints: Simplify each radical, then multiply it by its coefficient.

solutionReview.headline: Simplify, then combine like radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding radicands (√45 + √80 + √20 is not √145): only coefficients of like radicals add.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which radicals can be combined by adding their coefficients?
options: Like radicals, with the same index and radicand
scaffold.correct: Like radicals, with the same index and radicand

hints: A square root times itself is its radicand: √3 · √3 = 3.
Multiply different radicals with the Product Property: √a · √b = √(ab).
No two of the four terms are like radicals.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is √3 · √3?

solutionReview.headline: FOIL, then combine only like terms.
reasoning: No two terms are like radicals, so the product is 6√3 − 6 + 9√5 − 3√15.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding 6√3 and 9√5: only like radicals combine.

questions.prompt: In a square with side $a$, the ratio of a side to the difference between the diagonal and a side is $\dfrac{a}{a\sqrt{2} - a}$. Use a conjugate to rationalize the denominator and simplify.

responses.label: Factor the denominator: a√2 − a = a(…), with … =

steps.title: Conjugates
steps.instruction: a√b + c√d and a√b − c√d are conjugates. Their product has no radicals: (√2 − 1)(√2 + 1) = 2 − 1 = 1.

steps.title: Rationalize a binomial denominator
steps.instruction: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.

hints: Factor a out of the denominator, then cancel it with the numerator.
Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

solutionReview.headline: Divide out a, then multiply by the conjugate.
solutionReview.commonError: Cancelling a with one term of the denominator: a/(a√2 − a) is not 1/(√2 − a), because a must come out of both terms first, as a(√2 − 1).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Multiplying a binomial by its conjugate removes the radicals because…
options: the square roots add to zero

questions.prompt: Why simplify? Sort each expression: is it already in simplest radical form, or does it still need simplifying?
hints: Check each rule: smallest index, no nth-power factor, no fraction under the radical, no radical in a denominator, like radicals combined.
Could the index be smaller? Does any radicand have a perfect-power factor?

solutionReview.headline: Check every simplest-form rule.
reasoning: Simplest: 3√2, 2∛(3x), √3/3 and x√(xy)/y⁴. None has a perfect-power factor, a fraction under a radical, a radical in a denominator or an index that could be smaller.
solutionReview.commonError: √3/3 is simplified: its radical is in the numerator.

hints: Find the largest perfect square that divides {{R}}, and split a^{{e}} into an even power times a.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To simplify a square root, which factor of the radicand do you take out?

solutionReview.headline: Take out the largest perfect square.
solutionReview.commonError: Taking out a smaller square leaves a perfect-square factor under the radical.

hints: y¹¹ = y¹⁰ · y.
Find the largest perfect square that divides 240.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Under a square root, how do you split an odd power such as y¹¹?
options: An even power times one more y
scaffold.correct: An even power times one more y

solutionReview.headline: Take out the largest perfect square from each.
solutionReview.commonError: 240 = 4 · 60 leaves 60 = 4 · 15 still under the radical: take out 16 at once.

questions.prompt: Simplify $2\sqrt{75x^2y^3}$. The variable $x$ can be any real number.
hints: Find the largest perfect square that divides 75, and split y³ into y² · y.
√(x²) = |x|. Why does y need no bars?

solutionReview.headline: Pull out the squares.
reasoning: y³ under a square root forces y ≥ 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing 10xy√(3y): x may be negative, and a square root never is.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For every real number x, √(x²) equals…

hints: Rationalize: multiply the first by √y/√y.
For the second, multiply the top and the bottom so the denominator becomes a perfect cube.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √(x³/y⁷) has a fraction under the radical. Is it in simplest form?

solutionReview.headline: Simplify, then rationalize each denominator.
reasoning: ∛(8/(3y²)) = 2/∛(3y²). Multiplying by ∛(9y)/∛(9y) makes the denominator ∛(27y³) = 3y, so the result is 2∛(9y)/(3y).
solutionReview.commonError: A cube-root denominator needs a perfect cube under it, not a perfect square.

hints: Multiply the coefficients, multiply the radicands, then simplify the cube root.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In 3∛(16a²) · 2∛(4a), what do you do with the 3 and the 2?

solutionReview.headline: Multiply the coefficients, then the radicands.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the coefficients 3 and 2 instead of multiplying them.

hints: Find the largest perfect square that divides each radicand.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Can 15√3 and −8√3 be combined?

solutionReview.headline: Simplify each radical, then combine like radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting the last term: √3 is 1√3 and counts in the sum.

hints: Find the largest perfect square that divides {{P}}.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Before two radicals can be combined, what must they have in common?

solutionReview.headline: Simplify the first radical, then combine.
solutionReview.commonError: √{{P}} and √{{k}} become like radicals only after √{{P}} is simplified.

hints: FOIL gives four products; then combine only like radicals.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. How many products does FOIL give for two binomials?

solutionReview.headline: FOIL each product; combine only like radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: √5 · √7 is √35, not √12: radicands multiply.

hints: Combine the whole numbers and the like radicals.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What is (2√5)(4√5)?

solutionReview.headline: FOIL, then combine.

questions.prompt: Rationalize each denominator and simplify: $\dfrac{x}{x\sqrt{3} + x}$ and $\dfrac{5}{5\sqrt{3} + 6}$.
hints: Divide out x first, then multiply by the conjugate of the denominator.
The product of conjugates (a + b)(a − b) is a² − b².

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. To rationalize a denominator such as 5√3 + 6, multiply the top and bottom by…

solutionReview.headline: Simplify, then multiply by the conjugate.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate changes the value: multiply the numerator too.

hints: Write it as one square root and reduce the fraction inside.
A radical left in the denominator is not simplest form: rationalize it.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. √44/√33 can be written as one square root of…

solutionReview.headline: Write one radical, reduce, then rationalize.
solutionReview.commonError: 2/√3 is not simplest form: a radical is left in the denominator.

questions.prompt: Sort each expression: simplest radical form, or not yet simplified?
hints: Check each rule in turn: smallest index, no perfect-power factor, no fraction or radical in a denominator, like radicals combined.

solutionReview.headline: Check every simplest-form rule.
solutionReview.commonError: (√6 + 1)/5 is simplified: the radical is in the numerator and 6 has no square factor.

questions.prompt: The length $L$, in meters, of a fish of mass $M$ kilograms is modeled by $L = 0.46\sqrt[3]{M}$. Find the length of a fish with mass 30 kilograms, to the nearest hundredth of a meter.
hints: ∛30 ≈ 3.107. Multiply by 0.46 and round to hundredths.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In L = 0.46∛M with M = 30, what do you do first?

solutionReview.headline: Substitute, take the cube root, then multiply.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying 0.46 by 30 before taking the cube root gives about 2.40, which is not the model.

solutionReview.headline: Take out the largest perfect square.
solutionReview.commonError: An odd power such as b^{{eb}} leaves one factor of b under the radical.

solutionReview.headline: Simplify each radical, then combine like radicals.
solutionReview.commonError: √{{P}} and √{{Q}} are like radicals only after both are simplified.
